lines.trans: Hello, today we are going to do makeup that promises to wake even the dead.
Folks, for skin I like to use this one that is very dry.
And for the corpse I like to use my grandma, who is also very dry.
Do you have it handy, Grandma?
Just kidding, folks, we crack up back home with these jokes.
Well, speaking seriously now, wash your little face, okay?
Put on the moisturizer.
And then we start doing the skin.

meanings.note: Friendly greeting across Portuguese.

examples.text: Olá, hoje nós vamos fazer uma maquiagem.
examples.trans: Hello, today we are going to do makeup.

meanings.note: On the present day.

examples.text: Eu só tinha hoje livre mesmo.
examples.trans: I only had today free, really.
What are we going to do today?

meanings.note: First-person plural pronoun used after prepositions like pra.
Vou + infinitive can express a future intention: vou estar means I am going to be. Você takes the third-person vai.
Irregular past eu fiz (I made/did); não tem o que fazer means having nothing to do.

examples.text: Ela não tem o que fazer agora.
examples.trans: She has nothing to do now.

examples.text: Esse slide aqui eu fiz ontem.
examples.trans: This slide here I made yesterday.

meanings.note: Indefinite article; plural uns and umas mean some or a few in everyday Brazilian Portuguese.

examples.trans: Shall we have a little coffee?

meanings.note: Cosmetics applied to the face.

examples.text: A maquiagem eu até consigo tirar.
examples.trans: The makeup I can manage to take off.

meanings.note: All-purpose connector, relative link, question opener, and comparative word after mais or melhor.

examples.text: Eu acho que ele já foi.
examples.trans: I think that he already left.

meanings.note: Followed directly by an infinitive or que.

examples.text: Prometo não tomar o seu tempo.
examples.trans: I promise not to take up your time.

meanings.note: In levantar defunto, literally means to raise the dead.

examples.trans: It promises to wake even the dead.
I get up early every day.

meanings.note: In até logo it looks ahead to the next meeting. The phrase is added as the lesson farewell, not quoted from the selected source window.
Colloquial word for a dead person, as in the idiom levantar defunto (wake the dead).

examples.trans: It promises to wake even the dead.

examples.text: O café está forte para levantar defunto.
examples.trans: The coffee is strong enough to wake the dead.

meanings.note: Alone as vocative gente! it means folks/guys; with article a gente it means we/us with third-person singular verbs.

examples.text: Você acha que é melhor que a gente?
examples.trans: Do you think you're better than us?
Oh, folks, the meeting ran late.

meanings.note: Informal reduced para. Before a feminine noun, this Brazilian spelling can also represent a contraction including the article a; the exact meeting is clear from context.

examples.trans: Are you going to the meeting?

meanings.note: Human skin; fazer a pele means prepping the complexion in makeup.

examples.text: Pra pele eu gosto de usar esse.
examples.trans: For skin I like to use this one.

meanings.note: Subject form referring to the speaker. Explicit eu introduces his department in the explanation.
Conditional eu gostaria softens a refusal (I would like to, but...).

examples.trans: I would like to, but I have work.

meanings.note: Links a meeting with its subject. Do is de + the masculine article o; sou do financeiro identifies membership in the finance department.
Covers both using a tool/organ and wearing clothes.

examples.text: Essas camisas que a gente usa têm botão.
examples.trans: These shirts that we wear have a button.
Did my husband use all of this?

meanings.note: Demonstrative determiner; in spoken Brazilian Portuguese esse commonly covers both this near me and that just mentioned.

examples.text: Esse slide aqui eu fiz ontem.
examples.trans: This slide here I made yesterday.

examples.text: Vou ficar sentado esse tempo inteiro.
examples.trans: I'm going to stay seated that whole time.

meanings.note: Used for identifying a type of meeting or the department a person belongs to. The present forms sou and é are irregular.
Modifies a verb to mean well or carefully, as in olhar bem (look closely).

examples.text: Se vocês olharem bem, tem números.
examples.trans: If you look closely, there are numbers.

meanings.note: Diminutive of seco (dry), used in beauty tutorials for a non-oily matte finish.

examples.trans: Look, it stays nice and dry.
The skin stays nice and matte.

meanings.note: Coordinating conjunction pronounced [i] in natural Brazilian speech.

examples.text: Ela faltou e adiantou o trabalho.
examples.trans: She missed it and got ahead on her work.
There are good and bad numbers.

meanings.note: Dead body; plural cadáveres.

examples.text: Pro cadáver eu gosto de usar esse.
examples.trans: For the corpse I like to use this one.

meanings.note: Definite article agreeing in gender and number with its noun; also common before given names in casual Brazilian speech.

examples.trans: Look at the young woman over there.

meanings.note: First-person singular possessive agreeing with the thing possessed.

examples.text: O seu tempo vale mais que o meu?
examples.trans: Is your time worth more than mine?

meanings.note: Warm informal short form of avó (grandmother).

examples.text: A minha vó também tá aqui.

examples.trans: Do you have it handy, Grandma?

meanings.note: Adds another person or item to what was already stated.

examples.trans: I want you to go in too.
I'm the one who made it too!

meanings.note: Used here for being present at an event. Vou estar keeps estar in the infinitive after the finite form vou.

examples.trans: I’m not going to be at that meeting.
Are you going to be at that meeting?

meanings.note: Usually contracts with definite articles to no, na, nos, nas.
In tá na mão, colloquial Brazilian phrase for having something ready or handy.

examples.trans: Do you have it handy, Grandma?

examples.text: O documento já tá na mão.
examples.trans: The document is already in hand.

meanings.note: Used alone as Brincadeira! to mean 'Just kidding!'
In the Brazilian slang idiom cascar o bico, means to burst out laughing.

examples.text: A gente casca o bico lá em casa.

meanings.note: Colloquial Brazilian term for temporary or secondary work beside a main job.

examples.trans: It is my chiropractic side hustle.

examples.text: Ele faz bico de garçom à noite.
examples.trans: He works a side gig as a waiter at night.

meanings.note: Points to a place away from the speaker; lá dentro reinforces inside there.
Means both a house building and home.

examples.text: Vou voltar pra casa da minha mãe.
examples.trans: I am going to go back to my mother's house.

meanings.note: Marks accompaniment or an added ingredient such as sweetener.

examples.text: Ela está com a nossa equipe.

meanings.note: A funny story or one-liner.

examples.text: A gente ri com essas piadas.

meanings.note: Everyday adjective in tá bom (okay), boa tarde (good afternoon), and Bom, pessoal (Well, folks).
Covers speaking, talking, and telling in everyday Brazilian speech.

examples.text: Deixa eu te falar uma coisa.

examples.trans: They say a lot of things.

meanings.note: Used standalone as an incredulous question: Sério? (Seriously?).
Marks the current moment resulting from an earlier action.

examples.trans: Now she is in a meeting.

examples.text: Agora tenho que resolver umas coisinhas.
examples.trans: Right now I have to sort out a few little things.

meanings.note: Everyday verb for washing hands, face, or clothes.

examples.trans: I am going to wash my hands.

meanings.note: Affectionate diminutive of rosto (face) with -inho.
Passar impune means to go unpunished; passar por means to undergo.

examples.text: Eles passam por muitos testes lá.
examples.trans: They go through many tests there.

meanings.note: Skin moisturizing cream or lotion.

examples.trans: Put the moisturizer on your face.

meanings.note: Adds immediacy after imperatives like calma aí, or means there near you.
Takes a before an infinitive: começa a fazer (starts doing).

examples.text: A gente começa a fazer a pele.

meanings.note: Links verbs like faltar to an event or destination.
In the farewell até logo it anticipates meeting again. This is the time adverb, not a short form for a company logo.

examples.trans: I’ll go to the meeting soon.
